opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really at the heart of a lot of the work we've been doing on joint-embedding predictive architectures, things like I-JEPA and V-JEPA.

The way I think about it is: what do you actually want the model to learn? If you train a model to predict pixels, you're asking it to account for every detail in the input — the exact texture of the grass, the precise pattern of leaves moving in the wind, sensor noise. A lot of that is fundamentally unpredictable, and much of it isn't useful for understanding the scene. So a pixel-reconstruction model ends up spending a big chunk of its capacity modeling low-level details, and the representations it learns tend to need a fair amount of fine-tuning before they're useful for semantic tasks.

When you predict in representation space instead, you give the model the freedom to discard information that isn't predictable. If you mask out part of an image or a video clip and ask the model to predict the *embedding* of that region, it can focus on the higher-level stuff: there's a dog here, its head is probably over there, this object is moving in this direction. That tends to give you more semantic features, and in our experiments those features work well even with a frozen backbone and just a lightweight probe on top. It's also more efficient: you're not decoding full-resolution outputs, so training converges faster in terms of compute.

Of course, there's a trade-off. Predicting encodings opens the door to representation collapse: the model could trivially map everything to a constant and get perfect predictions. So you need architectural choices to prevent that, like an exponential moving average target encoder, a stop-gradient, and a careful masking strategy so the prediction task is actually challenging. With pixels you get that grounding for free because the target is fixed.

And it depends on your end goal. If you actually need to generate images or video, then you need a pixel decoder at some point. But if your goal is perception, understanding, or eventually planning in a world model, I'd argue you want to do prediction in an abstract representation space. That's closer to how we think humans reason: we don't imagine the future at the pixel level, we predict at a more abstract level of what's going to happen.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel prediction must model low-level details, many of which are unpredictable and not useful, making it a reason to predict embeddings instead.

r002.rationale: It says image or video generation requires a pixel decoder, but does not judge pixel prediction appropriate for producing visually appealing content.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the crux of the whole thing for me. When you train a model in pixel space, you're asking it to reconstruct every single detail of the input, and a lot of those details are just not semantically meaningful. If I show you a picture of a dog on grass, and I ask you to predict the exact configuration of every blade of grass, you're spending an enormous amount of model capacity on something that's essentially unpredictable noise. There's no way to know where each blade is going to fall, and it doesn't matter for understanding the image.

So the problem with pixel-level prediction is that the loss doesn't distinguish between information that matters and information that doesn't. The model has to care about all of it equally, and in practice what you get is representations that are very good at low-level texture and local statistics, but you have to do a lot of work downstream, fine-tuning or large probes, to pull out the semantic content.

The idea behind predicting in representation space, which is what we do with I-JEPA and now V-JEPA, is that you let the model decide what's worth predicting. You have a context encoder that looks at part of the input, a target encoder that looks at the rest, and the predictor's job is to predict the target's embeddings, not its pixels. Because the target encoder is also learned, the representation can throw away the unpredictable stuff. It can abstract away the exact blades of grass and keep "this region is grass, it's textured, it's green." That's an abstraction the model arrives at on its own because that's what's actually predictable from context.

Of course, the obvious worry is collapse. If both encoders can learn anything, the trivial solution is to output a constant, and then prediction is perfect and useless. So a lot of the design is about preventing that. We use an exponential moving average for the target encoder, and importantly we use a multi-block masking strategy with fairly large, semantically meaningful targets so the task is hard enough that the model actually has to learn something about the world to solve it. That masking design turned out to matter a lot more than we initially expected.

What I'd say in terms of the tradeoff is, pixel prediction gives you a very well-defined, stable objective, and it's hard to argue with, you know exactly what you're optimizing. But you pay for that in sample efficiency and in the quality of the abstraction. Representation-space prediction is harder to get right, there are more moving parts, but when it works you get a model that's learned something closer to a world model, where it's modeling the predictable structure of the world rather than memorizing surface statistics. And empirically, we see that in the frozen evaluations: you can take the encoder, not fine-tune it at all, and get strong performance on things like object recognition or action recognition in video, which tells you the semantics are already there in the features.

The way I think about it from a more philosophical angle is, we don't perceive the world by predicting photons hitting our retinas. We predict at a level of abstraction. And so if the goal is to build systems that understand the world rather than just reproduce it, I think the objective should live at that abstract level too.

r001.rationale: The response says pixel prediction must reconstruct semantically irrelevant, unpredictable details such as individual grass blades, while representation prediction can abstract those details away.

r002.rationale: It describes pixel prediction as a stable, well-defined objective, but does not say it is appropriate for generating visually appealing content.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what do you want the model to learn? If you predict pixels, you're asking it to account for a lot of detail—the exact texture of a surface, the lighting, things that might not matter for understanding what's happening in the scene. And when you're predicting the future, many of those details are inherently unpredictable. There can be lots of plausible futures.

Predicting in a representation space gives you the opportunity to abstract away some of that detail and focus on the underlying structure. You might care that an object is moving in a particular direction, without needing to predict exactly what every pixel of that object will look like.

But the challenge is that you have to learn a good representation. If the encoder just outputs a constant, prediction becomes trivial, but you've learned nothing. So you need a learning setup that avoids that collapse and preserves useful information.

I wouldn't say one is universally better. If your goal is to generate images, pixels are ultimately important. If your goal is to learn representations for understanding and prediction, then predicting encodings is a very appealing approach.

r001.rationale: It says pixel prediction requires modeling fine detail that may not matter and can be inherently unpredictable, while encoding prediction can focus on underlying structure.

r002.rationale: It says pixels are ultimately important when the goal is to generate images, which communicates that pixel prediction suits image generation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what do you want the model to learn? If you predict pixels, you’re asking it to account for every detail of an observation, including things that may be difficult to predict and irrelevant to the task. In a video, that could be the exact texture of a surface or the motion of leaves in the background.

Predicting in a representation space gives you the opportunity to abstract away some of that detail and focus on the underlying structure—what objects are present, how they interact, how the scene evolves. But the challenge is that you have to learn that representation. If the encoder just outputs a constant, prediction becomes very easy, but you haven’t learned anything useful. So the learning setup has to prevent that kind of collapse.

I wouldn’t frame it as pixels always being the wrong target. If you want to generate images, those details matter. But if your goal is to learn representations for understanding and prediction, you may not need to reconstruct every pixel to get there.

r001.rationale: It says pixel prediction must account for every detail, including details that are difficult to predict, while representation prediction can abstract them away.

r002.rationale: It says image generation makes pixel details matter, but does not clearly identify visually appealing content as the goal for which pixel prediction is appropriate.
